bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Chapter 3: Linear Models for Regression

question: How can continuous targets be predicted with models linear in their parameters, and how are model complexity and hyperparameters controlled by regularisation, the bias-variance view, and a Bayesian treatment?
contributions: Linear basis function models, maximum likelihood = least squares, normal equations, geometry, LMS, ridge/lasso regularisation, multiple outputs (3.1)
Frequentist bias-variance decomposition with sinusoidal simulation (3.2)
Bayesian linear regression: posterior, predictive distribution, equivalent kernel (3.3)
Bayesian model comparison and evidence (3.4); evidence approximation with re-estimation of alpha and beta and effective number of parameters (3.5)

limits: Bias-variance decomposition is of limited practical value: it needs an ensemble of data sets while in practice there is one (p.152).
Linear models have significant limitations for high-dimensional inputs; fixed basis functions suffer the curse of dimensionality (3.6, p.173).
Gaussian noise assumption makes p(t|x) unimodal (p.141).
Localised-basis Bayesian model is overconfident away from basis centres (p.158).
Model evidence is sensitive to the prior and undefined for improper priors; keep an independent test set (p.164-165).
Evidence approximation sets hyperparameters to point values; full marginalisation is intractable (p.165). Laplace alternative reported poorer (MacKay 1999).
No real-data experiments; all illustrations are synthetic (sinusoid, straight line). No code is given.
practices: Treat regression as maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise: minimise sum of squares and solve normal equations w=(Phi^T Phi)^-1 Phi^T t (3.1.1, p.142).
Use SVD rather than the normal equations when Phi^T Phi is near singular, and note a regulariser guarantees non-singularity (3.1.2, p.143).
Use stochastic gradient descent (LMS) for large or streaming data, choosing the learning rate with care (3.1.3, p.144).
Add a quadratic (weight decay) penalty, w=(lambda I+Phi^T Phi)^-1 Phi^T t; use q=1 (lasso) for sparsity (3.1.4, p.144-145).
Fit multiple targets with a shared design matrix: one pseudo-inverse serves all outputs (3.1.5, p.147).
Do not choose lambda by minimising the regularised error jointly with w; that gives lambda=0 (p.147).
Choose complexity by hold-out data or, preferably, by the model evidence which uses training data alone (3.3, 3.5).
Iterate alpha=gamma/(m_N^T m_N) and 1/beta=(1/(N-gamma)) sum(t-m_N^T phi)^2 until convergence; eigenvalues of Phi^T Phi are computed once (3.5.2, p.169).
When N >> M use gamma=M shortcuts alpha=M/(2 E_W(m_N)), beta=N/(2 E_D(m_N)) (p.171).
Keep an independent test set to evaluate the final system even when using Bayesian model comparison (p.165).

terms.definition: fixed nonlinear functions phi_j(x) whose linear combination gives the model
the parameter w0 that allows for any fixed offset in the data (not to be confused with bias in a statistical sense)
N x M matrix Phi with elements Phi_nj = phi_j(x_n)
the sum-of-squares regulariser (1/2) w^T w, encouraging weights to decay towards zero unless supported by data
regulariser with q = 1 in (3.29); a large enough lambda drives some coefficients to zero giving a sparse model
squared bias: extent to which the average prediction over data sets differs from the regression function; variance: extent to which individual-data-set solutions vary around their average
k(x,x') = beta phi(x)^T S_N phi(x'), so y(x,m_N) = sum_n k(x,x_n) t_n
p(D|M_i), the likelihood with the parameters marginalised out
the ratio of model evidences p(D|M_i)/p(D|M_j)
